title: DIC: Clotting and Bleeding at the Same Time
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Disseminated intravascular coagulation is a secondary syndrome of widespread coagulation activation that consumes platelets and clotting factors, causing both microvascular thrombosis and serious bleeding. Treat the underlying cause while supporting perfusion and hemostasis.
recognize: Oozing from IV sites, mucosal bleeding, petechiae, bruising, hematuria, GI bleeding, or shock may occur.
Laboratory patterns often include thrombocytopenia, prolonged coagulation studies, low fibrinogen, and elevated fibrin-degradation markers.
Sepsis, major trauma, obstetric catastrophe, and some malignancies are important triggers.
priorities: Assess ABCs, perfusion, active bleeding, neurologic status, urine output, and the underlying trigger.
Minimize unnecessary invasive procedures and venipunctures.
Administer ordered blood components and cause-directed therapy while monitoring response.
assessMonitor: Trend platelets, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, hemoglobin, renal function, urine output, skin/mucosal bleeding, and hemodynamics.
interventions: Apply prolonged direct pressure after invasive procedures.
Support sepsis, hemorrhage, or obstetric-emergency protocols depending on the cause.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulation is not a universal treatment for DIC and requires specialist direction based on the clinical pattern.
Avoid IM injections and medications that worsen bleeding when alternatives exist.
redFlags: Rapidly falling fibrinogen/platelets with clinical deterioration
teaching: Explain that DIC is caused by another serious illness and that treatment focuses on both the trigger and dangerous bleeding/clotting effects.
delegationScope: Routine output measurement may be delegated with strict reporting thresholds; bleeding and perfusion assessment require licensed-nurse judgment.
examTrap: Treating DIC as a simple low-platelet disorder without addressing the underlying sepsis, hemorrhage, trauma, or obstetric cause.
oneLinePearl: DIC consumes the clotting system: microclots inside, bleeding outside.
sourceBasis: International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis DIC Guidance

title: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia: Low Platelets, High Clot Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: HIT is an immune-mediated prothrombotic reaction to heparin. A substantial platelet fall after heparin exposure—especially with new thrombosis—requires stopping all heparin exposure and urgent evaluation for non-heparin anticoagulation.
recognize: HIT often appears several days after heparin starts but can occur sooner with recent prior exposure.
Thrombosis is the major danger; platelets may be low without spontaneous bleeding.
New DVT, PE, limb ischemia, skin necrosis, or abrupt circuit thrombosis can be clues.
priorities: Stop heparin products when HIT is suspected and notify the provider/RN immediately.
Check for hidden heparin sources such as flushes or coated devices according to policy.
Assess for thrombosis and prepare for ordered non-heparin anticoagulant therapy.
assessMonitor: Trend platelet count, signs of VTE/arterial thrombosis, skin findings, renal/hepatic function, and anticoagulant effects.
interventions: Use the facility's HIT risk-assessment and laboratory pathway.
Label/document the suspected or confirmed heparin reaction accurately in the medication record.
medicationSafety: Do not give more heparin simply because the patient is clotting.
Platelet transfusion is not routine for uncomplicated HIT and requires specialist direction.
teaching: Patients with confirmed HIT should tell future healthcare teams about the reaction and avoid heparin unless a specialist-directed exception applies.
delegationScope: Medication administration may be delegated only within licensure/policy; recognition of thrombocytopenia plus thrombosis requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Assuming the low platelet count means the main risk is bleeding rather than thrombosis.
oneLinePearl: HIT paradox: platelets fall while clot risk rises.
sourceBasis: American Society of Hematology HIT Guideline

title: Hemophilia: Protect Joints and Treat Bleeding Early
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Hemophilia causes impaired clot formation and can produce spontaneous or trauma-related bleeding, especially into joints and muscles. Suspected head, neck, abdominal, or major muscle bleeding needs urgent factor-directed treatment and evaluation.
recognize: Hemarthrosis causes joint pain, warmth, swelling, and reduced movement.
Deep muscle bleeding can compress nerves or vessels.
Head injury is high risk even when external bleeding is absent.
priorities: Assess location/severity of bleeding and trauma history.
Administer prescribed factor replacement or other hemophilia therapy promptly for significant bleeding.
Avoid unnecessary invasive procedures and apply prolonged pressure after venipuncture.
assessMonitor: Trend pain, swelling, neurovascular status, hemoglobin when indicated, treatment response, and inhibitor history.
interventions: Use rest, appropriate ice/compression/elevation only as directed for joint bleeds alongside factor therapy.
Coordinate care with a hemophilia treatment center for significant events.
medicationSafety: Avoid aspirin and many NSAIDs unless the hemophilia team specifically approves them.
IM injections may increase bleeding risk; use alternate routes when appropriate and prescribed.
teaching: Know the personal treatment plan, wear medical identification, and seek urgent care after significant trauma or suspected internal bleeding.
delegationScope: Routine activity assistance may be delegated, but suspected internal bleeding requires licensed-nurse assessment and hematology escalation.
examTrap: Waiting for visible external bleeding before treating a painful swollen joint or head injury in hemophilia.
oneLinePearl: Hemophilia bleeds hide in joints, muscles, and the brain—treat early.

title: Tumor Lysis Syndrome: Potassium, Phosphate, Uric Acid, Kidneys
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Tumor lysis syndrome can occur when rapidly dividing cancer cells break down, releasing potassium, phosphate, and nucleic-acid metabolites. The immediate dangers are hyperkalemic dysrhythmia, hypocalcemic symptoms, and acute kidney injury.
recognize: Risk is greatest with highly treatment-sensitive, high-burden malignancies such as some leukemias and lymphomas.
Nausea, weakness, muscle cramps, paresthesias, oliguria, seizure, or dysrhythmia may reflect metabolic deterioration.
Laboratory changes can develop before major symptoms.
priorities: Monitor rhythm, urine output, potassium, phosphate, calcium, uric acid, and renal function according to the oncology protocol.
Maintain ordered hydration and administer uric-acid-lowering therapy as prescribed.
Escalate hyperkalemia, seizure, oliguria, or dysrhythmia immediately.
assessMonitor: Use frequent chemistry and renal monitoring during high-risk treatment windows.
Trend fluid balance and avoid unnoticed volume overload during aggressive hydration.
interventions: Administer allopurinol or rasburicase according to risk and orders.
Prepare for renal replacement therapy if severe refractory metabolic abnormalities or renal failure develop.
medicationSafety: Rasburicase requires attention to G6PD deficiency because of hemolysis/methemoglobinemia risk.
Potassium-containing fluids or supplements may be inappropriate during active TLS unless specifically ordered.
teaching: During high-risk cancer treatment, report reduced urine, severe weakness, muscle cramps, palpitations, or confusion immediately.
delegationScope: Routine intake/output may be delegated with exact thresholds; metabolic changes require licensed-nurse interpretation and escalation.
examTrap: Treating nausea after chemotherapy as an isolated side effect while missing oliguria and rising potassium.
oneLinePearl: TLS dumps cell contents into blood—watch potassium and kidneys first.
sourceBasis: National Cancer Institute Tumor Lysis Syndrome Resources

title: Chemotherapy Extravasation: Stop the Infusion, Preserve the Line
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Vesicant chemotherapy extravasation can cause severe tissue necrosis. Stop the infusion immediately, leave the vascular access device in place for aspiration/antidote steps when protocol directs, notify the oncology team, and use drug-specific warm/cold compress and antidote guidance.
recognize: Pain, burning, swelling, blanching, erythema, resistance, leaking, or loss of blood return during vesicant infusion are warning signs.
Central-line extravasation may present less obviously than peripheral infiltration.
Tissue injury can progress after the infusion stops.
priorities: Stop the medication infusion immediately.
Do not automatically remove the catheter before the extravasation protocol is reviewed.
Notify the oncology team and identify the exact drug, dose, site, and estimated volume.
assessMonitor: Mark/measure the affected area, assess pain, color, swelling, blistering, neurovascular status, and photograph/document per policy.
interventions: Aspirate residual drug through the existing access device when the protocol directs.
Apply drug-specific compresses and antidotes, then arrange follow-up because tissue injury may evolve.
medicationSafety: Warm versus cold compress depends on the specific vesicant; do not use one generic rule.
Anthracycline extravasation may be treated with dexrazoxane under an established protocol.
teaching: Tell patients to report burning, pain, tightness, or swelling immediately during chemotherapy infusion.
delegationScope: Vesicant chemotherapy administration and extravasation management require specially trained licensed staff according to state/facility policy.
examTrap: Removing the IV immediately and applying the same compress used for every infiltrated medication.
oneLinePearl: Chemo extravasation: stop drug, keep access for protocol, treat the specific agent.
sourceBasis: National Cancer Institute Extravasation and Vesicant Extravasation Resources

title: Malignant Spinal Cord Compression: New Back Pain Plus Weakness Is Urgent
bottomLine: In a patient with cancer, new severe back pain plus weakness, sensory change, gait difficulty, or bowel/bladder dysfunction may signal spinal cord compression. Early recognition and urgent imaging/treatment are critical to preserving neurologic function.
recognize: Pain may be localized or radicular and can worsen when lying flat, coughing, or straining.
Weakness and gait difficulty often precede complete paralysis.
Urinary retention/incontinence or saddle sensory changes are late and concerning.
priorities: Perform focused neurologic assessment and report new weakness, sensory loss, or sphincter change immediately.
Use fall precautions and avoid unsupported ambulation.
Prepare for urgent MRI and corticosteroid/radiation/surgical management as ordered.
assessMonitor: Trend motor strength, sensation, gait, pain, bowel/bladder function, and level of the suspected lesion.
interventions: Maintain safe alignment and mobility precautions until spinal stability is known.
Coordinate urgent oncology, radiation oncology, or neurosurgical evaluation.
medicationSafety: High-dose corticosteroids may be used in selected cases and require glucose, GI, infection, and mental-status monitoring.
Do not mask rapidly progressive neurologic decline with repeated sedatives/opioids without reassessment.
teaching: Patients with cancer should report new severe back pain or neurologic symptoms promptly rather than waiting for routine follow-up.
delegationScope: Routine mobility assistance may be delegated, but new neurologic deficits require immediate licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Treating new severe back pain in a patient with metastatic cancer as routine musculoskeletal pain without a neurologic assessment.
oneLinePearl: Cancer + new back pain + weakness/bladder change = spinal cord emergency.
sourceBasis: National Cancer Institute Spinal Cord Compression Resources

title: Superior Vena Cava Syndrome: Upper-Body Venous Obstruction
bottomLine: Superior vena cava syndrome causes impaired venous return from the head, neck, and upper extremities. Facial/neck swelling, distended neck or chest veins, arm edema, dyspnea, cough, or neurologic symptoms in a patient with thoracic cancer or central venous devices require prompt evaluation.
recognize: Symptoms may worsen when lying flat or bending forward.
Plethora, cyanosis, hoarseness, dysphagia, headache, or confusion can occur.
Lung cancer, lymphoma, or catheter-associated thrombosis are important causes.
priorities: Assess airway, breathing, neurologic status, head/neck/arm swelling, oxygenation, and ability to tolerate supine position.
Elevate the head of bed for comfort and venous drainage unless contraindicated.
Escalate stridor, severe dyspnea, cerebral symptoms, or hemodynamic compromise immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend respiratory effort, facial/upper-extremity edema, neurologic symptoms, venous distention, and treatment response.
interventions: Prepare for imaging and cause-directed therapy such as stenting, anticoagulation, radiation, or chemotherapy.
Avoid unnecessary upper-extremity venous procedures when severe obstruction makes access problematic and another route is ordered.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulation is used when thrombosis is present and requires bleeding-risk monitoring.
Diuretics or steroids are not universal definitive therapy for SVCS and should follow the cause-specific plan.
teaching: Report rapidly increasing facial/neck swelling, breathlessness, or neurologic symptoms urgently.
delegationScope: Positioning may be delegated, but respiratory and neurologic assessment requires licensed-nurse evaluation.
examTrap: Placing the patient flat for comfort despite worsening facial swelling and dyspnea.
oneLinePearl: SVCS backs blood up above the chest—head up, assess airway, escalate cause.
sourceBasis: National Cancer Institute Cardiopulmonary Syndromes PDQ: Superior Vena Cava Syndrome

title: Cancer Therapy Mucositis: Pain, Nutrition, Infection
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Oral mucositis from cancer therapy can impair nutrition, hydration, communication, and infection defense. Frequent gentle oral care, pain control, moisture, and early infection assessment are priorities.
recognize: Erythema, ulceration, burning pain, dry mouth, difficulty swallowing, and reduced intake are common.
Neutropenia increases the risk that oral lesions become portals for serious infection.
Candida or herpes infection may complicate treatment-related mucosal injury.
priorities: Inspect the mouth regularly and assess pain, swallowing, intake, weight, and infection signs.
Use gentle oral hygiene and prescribed rinses/analgesia.
Escalate inability to swallow fluids, uncontrolled pain, fever, or rapidly spreading lesions.
assessMonitor: Trend oral intake, hydration, weight, lesion extent, fever, and blood counts when relevant.
interventions: Use a soft toothbrush if platelets permit and bland nonirritating foods/fluids as tolerated.
Coordinate nutrition support and speech/swallow evaluation when needed.
medicationSafety: Avoid alcohol-containing mouthwashes or caustic products on inflamed mucosa unless specifically ordered.
Topical anesthetics can impair protective sensation and swallowing; use according to instructions.
teaching: Perform oral care consistently and report mouth sores early rather than waiting until eating becomes impossible.
delegationScope: Routine oral care may be delegated when the plan is established; new lesions, fever, or swallowing change require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Using a harsh alcohol mouthwash because it feels more antiseptic on severely inflamed mucosa.
oneLinePearl: Mucositis threatens calories, fluids, and infection defense—not just comfort.
sourceBasis: National Cancer Institute Oral Complications of Cancer Therapies PDQ

title: Radiation Skin Care: Protect the Field, Do Not Scrub It
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Radiation dermatitis can cause erythema, dryness, itching, tenderness, and desquamation in the treatment field. Protect the skin from friction, heat, sun, and unapproved products while monitoring for moist breakdown or infection.
recognize: Skin changes are localized to the radiation field and can progress during treatment.
Moist desquamation is more severe than simple dryness and increases infection risk.
Treatment markings or immobilization guidance should not be scrubbed off.
priorities: Inspect the treatment field and assess pain, itching, drainage, and skin integrity.
Use gentle washing and pat dry unless the radiation team gives different instructions.
Report blistering, moist desquamation, severe pain, or infection signs.
assessMonitor: Trend skin changes across treatment sessions and after completion because reactions may peak later.
interventions: Use only creams, deodorants, dressings, or topical agents approved by the radiation team.
Protect the area from sun exposure and avoid heating pads/ice directly on the field.
medicationSafety: Topical corticosteroids or other agents may be prescribed; product choice and timing around treatment should follow radiation-oncology guidance.
teaching: Do not scrub, scratch, or apply new skin products to the treatment field without checking with the radiation team.
delegationScope: Routine hygiene assistance may be delegated; worsening skin injury requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Applying a heating pad or strong fragranced lotion to a painful radiation field without approval.
oneLinePearl: Radiation skin is fragile: gentle wash, no friction, no heat, approved products only.
sourceBasis: National Cancer Institute Radiation Therapy Side-Effect Guidance

title: Leukemia Supportive Care: Infection, Bleeding, Anemia
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Leukemia and its treatment can suppress normal marrow function, creating simultaneous risks from infection, bleeding, and anemia. PN care focuses on trend recognition, protective precautions, symptom support, and rapid escalation of fever, bleeding, or cardiopulmonary compromise.
recognize: Neutropenia increases infection risk, thrombocytopenia increases bleeding risk, and anemia reduces oxygen-carrying capacity.
Bone pain, fatigue, bruising, petechiae, recurrent infection, or lymphadenopathy may occur depending on disease type.
Treatment can also create tumor lysis and mucosal injury.
priorities: Assess temperature/infection signs, bleeding, dyspnea/fatigue, oral mucosa, and treatment complications.
Use neutropenic and bleeding precautions according to counts and oncology protocol.
Escalate fever, uncontrolled bleeding, new respiratory symptoms, or neurologic change immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend CBC with differential, platelets, hemoglobin, oral/skin sites, catheter sites, and treatment response.
interventions: Provide meticulous hand/oral hygiene and safe central-line care.
Balance activity with fatigue and transfusion/supportive care orders.
medicationSafety: Chemotherapy effects vary by regimen; verify drug-specific precautions rather than applying one generic toxicity profile.
Avoid rectal temperatures/procedures when severe neutropenia or thrombocytopenia makes mucosal injury unsafe.
teaching: Know the oncology team's fever and bleeding thresholds and report symptoms immediately rather than self-treating at home.
delegationScope: Routine hygiene and intake/output may be delegated with precautions; fever, bleeding, and treatment-toxicity assessment require licensed-nurse evaluation.
examTrap: Focusing only on the leukemia diagnosis and missing the immediate marrow-failure threats of infection, bleeding, and low oxygen delivery.
oneLinePearl: Leukemia supportive care asks three questions: infection? bleeding? oxygen delivery?
sourceBasis: National Cancer Institute Leukemia Treatment and Supportive Care Resources
